It then establishes C ≠ 0 using A ≠ 0, so degrees of B and C are defined. The leading-term argument correctly shows deg(BC) = deg(B) + deg(C), hence deg(A) = deg(B) + deg(C) ≥ deg(B). latest_nl_proof:
Let C(q) \in Z[q] be the polynomial such that A(q)/B(q)=C(q). Since B(q) is nonzero, multiplying this identity by B(q) gives A(q)=B(q)C(q). Also C(q) must be nonzero: if C(q)=0, then A(q)=B(q)C(q)=0, contradicting the hypothesis that A(q) is nonzero. Now set m=deg(B) and n=deg(C). Write B(q)=b_m q^m+b_{m-1}q^{m-1}+\cdots+b_0 with b_m
eq 0, and C(q)=c_n q^n+c_{n-1}q^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0 with c_n
eq 0. In the product B(q)C(q), the term q^{m+n} appears with coefficient b_m c_n. Because b_m and c_n are nonzero integers, their product b_m c_n is also nonzero. Moreover, every other term in the product comes from q^i\cdot q^j with i\le m and j\le n, and if (i,j)
eq (m,n), then i+j<m+n. Hence no term of degree larger than m+n occurs, and the coefficient of q^{m+n} is nonzero. Therefore deg(B(q)C(q))=m+n. Since A(q)=B(q)C(q), we get deg(A)=deg(B)+deg(C)\ge deg(B). Thus deg(A)\ge deg(B), as required.

statement_nl: Let A(q) and B(q) be nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. If the rational function A(q) / B(q) is itself a polynomial in Z[q], then deg(A) >= deg(B).

domain_restrictions: A is a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients
B is a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients
A divided by B is assumed to be a polynomial in Z[q], not merely a rational function
Degree is interpreted only for nonzero polynomials
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every pair of nonzero integer-coefficient polynomials A and B, if the quotient A divided by B is again an integer-coefficient polynomial, then the degree of A is greater than or equal to the degree of B.
quantifier_order: For all polynomials A and B in Z[q], if A and B are nonzero and A divided by B is a polynomial in Z[q], then deg(A) is at least deg(B).
witness_dependencies: The conclusion depends only on the given polynomials A and B
